extracted.intended_audience: brand managers, packaging designers, marketing teams, and creative agencies
extracted.subtask_description: A case-study style critique of a packaged goods redesign (Tropicana) highlighting what went wrong and lessons for future brand/packaging redesigns. Focus is on recognition, hierarchy, and research-driven decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: The images
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of the famous orange being punctured by the oversized straw eliminated the key visual cue customers scanned for on saturated shelves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the single most recognizable imagery that signals the product at-a-glance; losing that cue reduces shelf recognition and harms sales. Example: Tropicana's removed orange/straw image was the one thing customers looked for; without it people didn't recognise the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: The lid
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving the orange image from the primary carton to the lid made the identifying element less visible during normal shelf scanning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relocating primary identifiers to less prominent parts of the pack (e.g., lid) where they won't be seen during typical shopping behaviors. While novel engineering (a cap shaped like half an orange) can be creative, it may not compensate for reduced familiarity or visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: The logo
rubrics_metrics.description: Revamping the logo to a more modern typeface and rotating it to give the '100% Orange Pure and Natural' message priority altered the established visual identity that previously stood out on crowded shelves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious modernizing or reconfiguring logo and typographic treatments that have proven distinctiveness; changes that downgrade the brand mark's prominence can reduce recognition. Pay attention to visual hierarchy so the brand identifier remains clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity (central element)
rubrics_metrics.description: The redesigned packaging 'lacked one central element: familiarity.' Established brands must retain elements consumers associate with the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When redesigning an established brand, preserve familiar cues consumers rely on. Novelty should be balanced against existing mental models to avoid alienating loyal buyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and insight must drive decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: When redesigning packaging for an already established brand, data and insight must be the driving forces behind decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative and qualitative evidence to inform design choices (e.g., which elements are most salient to shoppers). Avoid purely aesthetic or internally driven changes without testing their impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world market and consumer research
rubrics_metrics.description: If the agency and Tropicana had done real-world market and consumer research, they would have found the aspects that consumers look for in the packaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct in-context testing (shelf tests, in-store observation, concept testing) to validate recognition and preference before rolling out a redesign. Research should identify which visual elements to carry across.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider competitive shelf context and salience
rubrics_metrics.description: Customers scanned a saturated shelf; competitors took advantage of the redesign failure and captured sales/market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the new design performs among competitors in the actual retail environment — salience against other products matters. A redesign that reduces distinctiveness can create openings for rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance creative innovation with proven cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative engineering (e.g., novel cap design) can be interesting but may not be enough if it fails to maintain the familiar cues shoppers rely on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovate where it adds functional or perceptual value, but do not replace core recognizers (imagery, logo placement) with novelty unless research shows equal or greater effectiveness. Prototype timeline: consider staged rollout or A/B tests to mitigate large-scale risk.
